Print this page

This guidance provides information on the qualification, compliance and notification requirements for the third compliance period (phase 3). The remaining deadline is to submit the second progress update report by 5 December 2026.

See the Comply with ESOS phase 4 guidance for information on the qualification, compliance and notification requirements for Phase 4.

Phase 4 guidance reflects the changes in the most recent amendment in the Energy Savings Opportunity Scheme Regulations 2014, as amended 2026.

About this guidance

This guidance is published by the Environment Agency as the UK scheme administrator for ESOS, on behalf of all the UK regulators which are:

Environment Agency for organisations whose registered office is in England
[...]
The scheme has resulted in estimated annual efficiency energy savings of 1.65 TWh from buildings,1.51 TWh savings for industrial processes, and 0.52 TWh of fuel efficiency savings across the ESOS population. (Data is from the ESOS post implementation review).

The changes to the scheme being introduced from the third compliance period onwards are estimated to lead to an additional 28 TWh across all participants over 2024 to 2037, which equates to an estimated £1.12 billion in energy bill savings for participants over that period. (Data is from the Energy Security Bill factsheet: Powers to strengthen the energy savings opportunity scheme).

[...]
Where there is no energy supply, the trust assets will not need to be included in an ESOS assessment because trust assets only fall into ESOS if an energy supply agreement is held. The concept of a supply agreement being in place only affects the qualification of trusts for ESOS, all other types of undertaking which meet the qualification criteria will be required to participate in ESOS if they meet the qualification criteria.

The table summarises how responsibility for ESOS compliance for a trust asset is determined.

Asset responsibility Arranges the supply of energy to the asset Qualifies for ESOS in their own right Include the asset as part of their own ESOS assessment Include the asset as a separate ESOS compliance notification
Dominant beneficiary Yes Yes Yes No
[...]
If a qualifying group sells an undertaking to an organisation that did not qualify for ESOS then the energy supplies of the purchaser do not need to be included in ESOS. Only the energy supplies of the undertaking that has been purchased will be subject to ESOS.

3. Deadlines
3.1 Compliance periods and compliance dates

Qualification is based on the status of your organisation on the relevant qualification date. If your organisation qualifies, you must participate in ESOS and notify compliance to the Environment Agency by the last date of each compliance period (‘the compliance date’).

[...]
If you believe that you will not meet the new extended compliance deadline for the third compliance period, please read section 15 on compliance and enforcement which outlines the steps you need to take.

3.2 Changes to the compliance date for the third compliance period

For the majority of ESOS purposes, the compliance date for the third compliance period is extended to 5 June 2024. In particular this applies to:

undertakings which leave a corporate group between the qualification date and the compliance date (section 2.8)
excluding assets from your total energy consumption which you no longer own (section 4.3.1)
the period for which data can be used for the energy audit (section 8.3)
producing the ESOS report (section 10)
submission of the compliance notification (section 12)
[...]
carry out energy audits or use alternative compliance routes for your areas of significant energy consumption or, as applicable, total energy consumption
complete the ESOS report
share the ESOS report, and any relevant documentation relating to alternative compliance routes, with group undertakings
get one or more directors to review the findings of the assessment
submit an ESOS notification of compliance through the online notification system (known as MESOS)
keep a record in your evidence pack of the ESOS notification of compliance (either by printing it or retaining an electronic copy), a copy of your ESOS report and any other records of the assessment
Changes for participants complying using ISO 50001

[...]
Participation in these other schemes does not automatically count as ESOS compliance for the energy covered by those regimes. You can use energy data you collect as part of your compliance with these schemes to calculate your total energy consumption for your ESOS assessment, but you are likely to have to do additional work to ensure you are also compliant with ESOS.

The scope of energy you must include in your total energy consumption under ESOS is broader than that covered by these mandatory and voluntary schemes. This means that it is unlikely you will be able to calculate your total energy consumption based on the data you collect for these schemes alone.

4.6 How to estimate

If you cannot get verifiable data, you can fill in the gaps by estimating data. To do this, you could use:

[...]
You must set out information in relation to the compliance routes used for your areas of significant energy consumption (or total energy consumption) in your ESOS report (see section 10). You must also keep records about the assessment in your evidence pack (section 11).

7.01 Energy audits

Previous audit work, for instance performed as part of other energy audit schemes, can be used towards compliance with ESOS provided they both:

were conducted within the compliance period (6 December 2019 – 5 December 2023 for the third compliance period)
meets the minimum requirements of an ESOS energy audit (see section 8)
7.02 Alternative compliance routes (ISO 50001, DEC, GDA)

[...]
8.1 Auditing areas of significant energy consumption or total energy consumption

You must carry out an energy audit of the participant’s areas of significant energy consumption (or total energy consumption, where you have chosen not to identify areas of significant energy consumption) unless they are covered by alternative route(s) to compliance.

You can do this specifically to comply with ESOS, or you can use previously undertaken energy audits to contribute to ESOS compliance provided they were not relied upon for ESOS compliance in any previous compliance period. You can use more than one energy audit to cover different areas of significant consumption (or, as applicable, total energy consumption) and these may cover different time periods.

[...]
analyse the participant’s energy consumption and energy efficiency using energy consumption profiles where appropriate and reasonably practicable (section 8.5)
identify measures for the participant to improve its energy efficiency (section 8.6)
recommend which of those measures are reasonably practical and cost-effective energy saving – these are termed energy saving opportunities (section 8.6)
categorise each energy saving opportunity (section 8.7)
estimate the costs and benefits of each energy saving opportunity (section 8.8)
identify considerations relevant to the implementation of each energy saving opportunity (section 8.9)
recommend a programme for implementing the energy savings opportunities (section 8.10)

ISO 14001 certified participants may use their certified environmental management system (EMS) to support ESOS compliance (section 8.11).

ESOS does not mandate specific energy auditing methodologies that must be used. Further guidance on some potential methodologies you may choose to use, for instance ISO 50002 or BS EN 16247, is included in Appendix C, section C4.4.

All energy audits must be reviewed by an ESOS lead assessor except where the participant’s total energy consumption is calculated to be less than 40,000 kWh (see section 7.2).

8.3 Energy consumption data

So far as reasonably practicable, you must base the energy audit on energy consumption data which:

is measured in energy measurement units and not by energy spend
is verifiable and evidences the participant’s energy consumption
covers a period of 12 consecutive months’ energy consumption

The 12-month period over which energy consumption is measured for each audit must:

begin no earlier than 12 months before the start of the compliance period (for the third compliance period it must begin no earlier than 6 December 2018)
begin no earlier than 24 months before the start of the ESOS energy audit by the participant in the compliance period (for example, for an ESOS energy audit which starts on 1 April 2023, data must begin no earlier than 1 April 2021)
end on or before the compliance date (that is, not extend beyond 5 June 2024 for the third compliance period)
not have been relied upon for energy audits for a previous compliance period

[...]
You must keep records in your evidence pack of the method used to make any estimates.

8.9 Information relevant to implementing energy savings opportunities

The energy audit must, so far as reasonably practicable, identify considerations relevant to implementing each energy saving opportunity, including, if applicable:

relevance of Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (as set out in the Energy Efficiency (Private Rented Property) (England and Wales) Regulations 2015) (“the MEES Regulations”) for privately rented domestic and non-domestic buildings used by the participant
availability of UK or devolved government funding to support implementation of energy savings opportunities
8.9.1 Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES) Regulations

[...]
ISO 14001 certified participants may wish to use their certified environmental management system (EMS) to support ESOS compliance. You can integrate ESOS compliance into the EMS by:

establishing objectives relating to energy use
providing a structure for capturing and managing relevant ESOS energy data as documented information
doing energy audits as part of an internal EMS audit programme that meet the minimum ESOS requirements described
making sure in-house energy managers are qualified and competent
sharing audit findings with top management though a forum
9. Using an alternative compliance route

This section provides information about alternative compliance routes that you can use in relation to ESOS compliance:

certified ISO 50001 energy management system (section 7 and 9.1) or
[...]
A DEC and its accompanying advisory report can only be used as a compliance route for the specific energy they both cover. For example, if any process energy used by a building is not considered by the advisory report, it would not be covered by the DEC compliance route for the purpose of ensuring at least 95% of total energy consumption (the significant energy consumption) is covered by a compliance route – see section 7.

Energy Performance Certificates (EPCs) are not a valid route for ESOS compliance. This is because EPCs are not based on the occupied energy consumption of the building, they are based on modelled consumption.

9.3 Green Deal Assessments

Green Deal Assessments (GDAs) are provided under the government’s Green Deal scheme for domestic and non-domestic buildings.

[...]
Where you describe any measure that relates to reducing your energy consumption under other mandatory or voluntary schemes, we recommend you refer to the name of the relevant non-ESOS scheme. You should ensure any measures (including any you have aggregated for the purpose of describing them as a single measure) are only recorded once. This will avoid double counting of the energy savings.

You may include only measures from other schemes that are proposed to be carried out during the relevant compliance period. Any measure which has already been carried out before the start of the relevant compliance period (6 December 2023 for the third compliance period) will not meet the requirements for inclusion.

findings.claim: Ofgem defines the main UK business energy contract types: fixed-rate, variable-rate, deemed-rate, out-of-contract, rollover/evergreen and flexible (structured). They differ in price certainty and risk.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: fixed-rate contracts "fix the price of unit rates and standing charges for the length of the contract", so the cost per kWh stays the same whatever happens to wholesale prices. With variable-rate contracts the price "can increase or decrease during the contract period", for example when wholesale prices change. Rollover/evergreen contracts renew automatically at the end of a fixed term if no new arrangement is made or no switch happens. The new term is usually 12 months and "may be on a higher rate". Ofgem also says suppliers may not offer all contract types.
findings.limitations: Ofgem's descriptions are brief. They give no figures on how much more deemed or out-of-contract rates cost. The page shows no date.

findings.claim: Deemed and out-of-contract rates are default states, not products you choose. They arise when no contract has been agreed, and they are usually more expensive than negotiated fixed-term contracts.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: you are put on a deemed contract automatically when you move into new premises without arranging a formal contract, and also if your supplier goes out of business. Deemed rates are "usually higher than negotiated contract rates". Some suppliers move you to out-of-contract rates if your fixed-term contract ends without a new deal, and these are also usually more expensive than fixed-term contracts. Ofgem advises checking what happens at contract end (auto-renewal, out-of-contract or deemed rates). GLCG (a broker/consultancy blog) says the same: deemed contracts apply when you move in without arranging a contract, and out-of-contract applies when a fixed term ends with no new deal. It adds that the supplier will often move you to a very expensive variable rate, and suggests starting to look for a new deal 3–6 months before expiry.
findings.limitations: GLCG is a commercial broker blog (published 2026-09-01) and is not a regulator source. Its 3–6 month advice is its own recommendation.

findings.claim: Fixed-term contracts give budget certainty but little flexibility. Variable contracts give flexibility but expose the buyer to market volatility. Flexible/pass-through contracts give the most control and the most risk. A "fixed" contract may not fix every part of the bill.
findings.evidence: GLCG on fixed contracts: they are typically 1–3 years, protect against wholesale spikes and make budgeting simple. The buyer does not benefit if prices fall, is locked in, and exit fees can be substantial. Many "fixed" contracts let suppliers pass on unexpected increases in non-commodity costs, so check for change-event or pass-through clauses. GLCG on variable contracts: the unit price follows wholesale market moves and is often adjusted monthly. The buyer can benefit from falls but faces surges that make budgeting hard. GLCG on flexible purchasing (pass-through) contracts: energy is bought in smaller blocks over the contract period, so the buyer can target market lows and costs are more transparent. These contracts need active management, carry higher risk and are not suitable for most SMEs. In a fully fixed contract the supplier bundles estimated non-commodity costs (network, levies) into the rate. In a pass-through contract they are charged at actual cost, which gives transparency but less budget certainty. Ofgem says flexible (structured) contracts suit large, high-usage businesses. Instead of locking in a price, they let companies buy energy in smaller portions when market conditions are better.
findings.limitations: The pros and cons come mainly from GLCG, a commercial source. Ofgem gives only a short description of flexible contracts. Neither source gives a precise regulatory definition of "pass-through" as distinct from "flexible".

findings.claim: Contracts can be arranged directly or through third-party intermediaries (brokers, consultants, price comparison sites). This brings cost-transparency and redress considerations, and there is no cooling-off period.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: you can arrange a contract yourself or use a broker, consultant or price comparison service (third-party intermediaries). Brokers charge, either an upfront fee or, more commonly, a commission paid by the supplier you choose. If a supplier pays the broker, the broker must belong to an approved redress scheme. Ofgem points to the Energy Ombudsman broker register and the UIA accredited list. Comparison sites may cover only part of the market and may earn commission. Ofgem also says: "there is no cooling-off period after you agree to your contract". It says to check whether broker fees or commissions are included in the price. GLCG says brokers can analyse consumption, explain contract structures, spot hidden charges and negotiate with several suppliers.
findings.limitations: Ofgem does not describe a separate "broker-brokered" contract type. Brokerage is a way of buying, and the underlying contract is still one of the types above.

findings.claim: Protections vary by business size. Microbusinesses get extra protections, mostly for evergreen contracts, so the risks of rollover and default rates differ by customer size.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: a microbusiness has fewer than 10 employees and turnover or balance sheet of no more than £2 million, or uses up to 100,000 kWh/year of electricity. Suppliers must give clear contract information and renewal price information before the contract ends. For evergreen contracts only, termination notice is limited to 30 days and requests to end must be acknowledged within 5 working days. Small and large businesses get different protections.
findings.limitations: Thresholds are as stated on the Ofgem page, which shows no date. Check current rules before relying on them.

findings.claim: Microbusinesses get specific protections at renewal and on ending a contract, but the notice-period and acknowledgement protections in Ofgem's guidance apply to evergreen contracts only.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: microbusiness suppliers must give clear contract information and renewal price information before the contract ends. For evergreen contracts only, termination notice is limited to 30 days and requests to end must be acknowledged within 5 working days. Citizens Advice: for a microbusiness on an evergreen (no end date) contract, you "might have to give up to 30 days' notice" before switching. Ofgem also says that a contract's end-of-term outcome (auto-renewal, out-of-contract or deemed rates) should be checked before agreeing.
findings.limitations: These are summaries of guidance, not licence condition text. Neither page cites SLC numbers. Small and large businesses get different, weaker protections. Ofgem's page shows no date.

findings.claim: Supplier renewal prompts, rollover periods and exit fees: for microbusinesses on fixed terms, suppliers should contact the customer about 3 months before the end. Once the fixed term has ended the customer can switch at any time without a fee or notice. Leaving early can mean an exit fee.
findings.evidence: Citizens Advice: "If your fixed term is ending soon, your supplier should let you know your switching options. They should contact you about 3 months before the end of your contract. If they don't, you can complain." If the fixed term has ended you can switch at any time with no fee and no notice. A contract may give a 'roll-over period' of no more than 12 months. Without one, or once it has ended, you are on an 'out-of-contract' tariff. You can switch from a roll-over period or out-of-contract tariff without a fee or notice. Switching before the end of a fixed term "might" mean an exit fee, so check when you can switch fee-free and whether the saving outweighs the fee. A deemed tariff also usually carries no switching fee or notice. Ofgem says rollover/evergreen contracts renew for a fixed term, usually 12 months, possibly at a higher rate.
findings.limitations: Citizens Advice's advice is framed for microbusinesses and for England. It gives no exit-fee amounts or calculation method, which are set by each contract. The page shows no date.

findings.claim: Switching process and contract formation: a business switch normally completes within 5 working days. There is no cooling-off period, and a verbal agreement can be binding.
findings.evidence: Citizens Advice: "You'll be switched to your new supplier within 5 working days", or on a specific date if requested. There is no cooling-off period when you switch, and "if you change your mind you might have to pay a termination fee". Business contracts are binding if agreed over the phone, so no signature is needed. Most business suppliers offer no cooling-off period. Ask for the contract in writing. Take meter readings on switch day and send them to both companies. Ofgem likewise says there is no cooling-off period after you agree a contract.
findings.limitations: The 5-working-day timeline is from Citizens Advice's consumer guidance. The task also asked about objection rights, and no source read covers supplier objections to a switch. The page shows no date.

findings.claim: Broker transparency rules: microbusinesses must be told broker pay before agreeing. Ofgem has extended broker-fee disclosure to all non-domestic customers, and requires redress-scheme membership for brokers on Small Business contracts.
findings.evidence: Citizens Advice: for microbusinesses working with a supplier-paid broker, the broker must disclose how much the supplier pays them before the contract is agreed. Terms and conditions, including any broker fee, should arrive within 10 days of agreeing. Brokers paid by the supplier must be registered with the Energy Ombudsman or UIA. Ofgem press release (5 April 2024): the requirement for a contract's principal terms to clearly display broker fees was to be expanded from Micro Business consumers to all non-domestic customers. It applies to contracts signed on and from 1 October 2024, and suppliers must make the information available on request. From December 2024 suppliers may only work with TPIs that are redress-scheme members when securing Small Business contracts.
findings.limitations: The Ofgem press release says some measures were "expected" by the end of 2024. It does not confirm they came into force, so check current licence conditions. The 10-day figure comes from Citizens Advice.

findings.claim: Ofgem Standards of Conduct now apply to all non-domestic customers, and dispute-resolution access was widened. Microbusiness and Small Business definitions are set out by Ofgem and in the press release notes.
findings.evidence: Ofgem press release (5 April 2024): from 1 July 2024 the Standards of Conduct were expanded to apply to all businesses of any size, not just Micro Business consumers. A new licence rule requires suppliers to signpost Micro Business consumers to Citizens Advice and Citizens Advice Scotland. This applies to Small Business consumers from December 2024, subject to the new definition entering legislation. Microbusiness: electricity use under 100,000 kWh a year, gas use under 293,000 kWh a year, or fewer than 10 employees with annual turnover not exceeding 2 million Euros (£1.716m on 22 March 2024). Small business (Energy Ombudsman coverage): fewer than 50 employees and £6.5 million turnover or £5 million balance sheet total, or 200,000 kWh electricity or 500,000 kWh gas a year. Ofgem's guidance page states the microbusiness test as fewer than 10 employees and turnover or balance sheet of no more than £2 million, or use of up to 100,000 kWh a year of electricity or 293,000 kWh a year of gas. Citizens Advice says microbusinesses get extra protections when switching.
findings.limitations: The press release is dated April 2024. The two Ofgem pages state the microbusiness definition slightly differently (Euro versus pound turnover, "less than" versus "up to" thresholds). Check the licence condition for the exact definition. No licence condition numbers are cited.

findings.claim: A business electricity bill splits into commodity costs (the energy itself, which tracks the wholesale market) and non-commodity costs (network, levies, supplier operating costs). Fixed contracts bundle the non-commodity costs into the rate, while pass-through contracts charge them at actual cost.
findings.evidence: GLCG: commodity costs are the price of the energy and "fluctuate with the wholesale market". Non-commodity costs include network maintenance fees, government levies for green initiatives and supplier operating costs, and can make up over half of the total bill. Bill line items include transmission and distribution charges (TNUoS and DUoS), balancing services (BSUoS), the Climate Change Levy (CCL), and Renewables Obligation (RO) and Feed-in Tariff (FiT) levies. "In a fully fixed contract, the supplier estimates these costs and bundles them into your rate. In a pass-through contract, these are charged at their actual cost, which provides transparency but reduces budget certainty." GLCG also warns that "fixed" does not always mean the whole bill is fixed. Many fixed contracts let suppliers pass on unexpected increases in non-commodity costs, so check for change-event or pass-through clauses. Ofgem says fixed-rate contracts fix unit rates and standing charges for the contract length, so the cost per kWh stays the same whatever wholesale prices do. It also says flexible (structured) contracts, for large users, buy energy in portions when market conditions are better.
findings.limitations: The component breakdown and the fixed versus pass-through treatment come from GLCG, a commercial consultancy blog. No Ofgem, NESO or network-operator page on business bill components was opened, so this is not an official breakdown. The percentage split of a bill and the exact negotiability of each element depend on the contract.

findings.claim: The Climate Change Levy applies to business (non-domestic) electricity and gas. HMRC publishes its rates by year, with reduced rates for Climate Change Agreement holders.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK (HMRC, last updated 27 Nov 2025): suppliers are responsible for charging the correct levy. The electricity main rate is £0.00775 per kWh from 1 April 2023 to 2025, £0.00801 from 1 April 2026 and £0.00827 from 1 April 2027. The gas rate is £0.00672 from April 2023, £0.00775 for 2024 and 2025, £0.00801 from April 2026 and £0.00827 from April 2027. Climate change agreement holders get a 92% discount on electricity, and 88% or 89% on gas depending on the year. Rates do not apply to domestic consumers or to charities for non-business use. The VAT notice adds that the levy is chargeable on industrial and commercial supply (agriculture, industry, commerce, public administration, other services). It excludes small amounts of energy (de minimis). The value of a supply for VAT purposes includes CCL where appropriate.
findings.limitations: The rate table was last updated 27 Nov 2025, so check GOV.UK for later changes. The 2026 and 2027 rates are as published on that page. The page does not say how contracts treat CCL, though tax changes are normally passed through.

findings.claim: VAT on business energy: the standing charge is treated as part of the supply for VAT purposes, so it takes the same VAT rate as the electricity. Qualifying use gets the reduced rate and non-qualifying use gets the standard rate. Pure network or meter charges made without a supply of electricity are standard-rated.
findings.evidence: HMRC VAT Notice 701/19: gas and electricity bills include a variable consumption charge and a fixed standing charge. "For VAT purposes it is regarded as part of the charge for a supply of gas or electricity, even though it is shown separately on bills." Where the supply is for qualifying use, the whole bill including the standing charge is taxed at the reduced rate. The supply of electricity for qualifying use is taxed at the reduced rate. Where a price covers electricity and standing or other charges, the whole supply takes the reduced rate. Charges for use of transmission or distribution lines, transformers or meters, without any supply of electricity, are always standard-rated. Wholesale electricity contracts are standard-rated. The page shows a temporary zero rate of VAT for domestic supplies and other qualifying use. It was announced on 21 July 2026 and extended at Budget 2026 from 31 March to 30 June 2027.
findings.limitations: The extract was shortened and the specific percentage rates were not visible in the text I read. I make no claim about the standard rate. The section defining "qualifying use" (section 3, de minimis and charity/domestic criteria) was omitted from the extract. The zero-rate announcement is described on the page as covering domestic supplies and other qualifying use, and it is unclear whether it covers ordinary business supplies. The page shows a last-updated date of 28 Oct 2026.

findings.claim: Ofgem does not license or regulate energy brokers (third-party intermediaries, TPIs). It sets voluntary principles and requires broker costs passed through the bill to be disclosed in the supplier's Principal Terms. Brokers paid directly by the business need not appear in those terms.
findings.evidence: Ofgem's TPI guidance (14 Oct 2022): "Ofgem do not regulate energy brokers" and "does not license TPIs but has set out voluntary principles": Honesty, Respect, Accuracy (say how much of the market was searched), Transparency (make the customer aware of all principal terms, including services and how they pay for them, directly or indirectly), Customer-focused (record and investigate complaints) and Professionalism. TPIs include switching sites, brokers and procurement firms. A TPI may be paid directly by the customer (flat fee, charge per trade) or indirectly, through a supplier payment added to the bill. TPI costs included in the supplier bill "must be provided to all businesses via the Principal Terms and upon request". Directly paid broker fees need not be declared in the supplier's principal terms. Supplier in-house sales teams need not disclose commission. Because commission is based on consumption, a customer who uses more than estimated pays on actual consumption. Ofgem advises asking a TPI which suppliers it will approach, how many offers it will give, what services it provides during the contract and how it is paid. TPIs must also comply with the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations, and Ofgem can seek court injunctions for breaches. Ofgem's 5 April 2024 press release adds that broker fees must be displayed in contracts' principal terms for all non-domestic customers, for contracts signed on and from 1 October 2024.
findings.limitations: The TPI guidance dates from October 2022, so some details may have changed (for example the 2024 expansion of disclosure to all non-domestic customers). Ofgem says it cannot require brokers to repay past undisclosed commission, and warns of scammers claiming otherwise. It notes recovery may be possible only through litigation (get independent legal advice).

findings.claim: Supplier-paid brokers must belong to a redress scheme (the Energy Ombudsman, the UIA or, per Citizens Advice, the DRO). A business should check registration before signing and be told in writing how the broker is paid.
findings.evidence: Citizens Advice: "If your broker is paid by your supplier they must be registered" with the Energy Ombudsman or the Utilities Intermediaries Association (UIA). Its problems page also lists the Dispute Resolution Ombudsman (DRO). "If your broker isn't registered you won't be able to complain." Each scheme's website has a register or accredited-member list. Microbusiness customers must be told what the supplier pays the broker before agreeing a contract. Terms should arrive within 10 days of agreeing. Phone agreements are binding, so ask for information in writing. Ofgem says: "Because there is no cooling-off period after you agree to your contract, it's important you make sure you use a trustworthy broker", and points to the Energy Ombudsman broker register and the UIA list. Ofgem says brokers' fees may be an upfront fee or, more usually, supplier commission.
findings.limitations: Citizens Advice mentions the DRO in one page and only the Energy Ombudsman and UIA in another, so the list may vary. Ofgem says it cannot approve redress schemes. The Citizens Advice pages show no date. Neither source gives UIA code-of-practice detail, as the UIA site was not read.

findings.claim: Complaint and escalation route: complain to the supplier or broker first, then the Energy Ombudsman after 8 weeks or a deadlock letter. Small businesses became eligible for broker and supplier disputes from 19 December 2024.
findings.evidence: Energy Ombudsman (page updated 2026-04-02): from 19 December 2024 small businesses can get free dispute resolution for disputes with a broker/TPI, where the business has fewer than 50 employees and turnover of at most £6.5 million or a balance sheet total of £5.0 million, or electricity use of no more than 200,000 kWh a year, or gas use of no more than 500,000 kWh a year. You must use the broker's or supplier's complaints process first. The Ombudsman can then help after 8 weeks or once a deadlock letter has been issued. Process: raise it with the broker, register the dispute, review any early resolution offer, evidence within 14 days, a decision, then 28 days for the broker to implement. Remedies: practical action, an apology, a payment of up to £10,000, and recommendations. It cannot fine or punish. It cannot rule on commercial decisions or on non-gas/electricity services such as LPG. It only handles brokers that have joined its scheme. Citizens Advice: for supplier complaints, 8 weeks or a deadlock letter, and 1 year from a deadlock letter to complain. Ofgem's April 2024 release says Small Businesses can resolve disputes about brokers with schemes such as the Energy Ombudsman and UIA, and that suppliers must signpost microbusinesses to Citizens Advice.
findings.limitations: The Energy Ombudsman page applies the eligibility test as quoted. It does not say whether a business must meet more than one criterion, though the wording uses "AND" and "OR". Citizens Advice's guidance is for England and for small and microbusinesses. Larger businesses may not qualify. Complaint wait times are those stated on each page.

findings.claim: Checking the supplier: Ofgem says a supplier is not obliged to supply a business and may choose customers by factors such as size or credit rating. Checks include contract end-of-term treatment and what happens if the supplier fails.
findings.evidence: Ofgem TPI guidance: "There is no obligation for a supplier to supply you – a supplier may determine which customers they choose to supply by factors such as size of supply or your credit rating." There are very few published business prices, so you need to ask suppliers for quotes. A contract can last multiple years and may have an early termination fee. Ofgem's business-contract page says you are placed on deemed rates if your supplier goes out of business, and to check what happens at the end of the contract. Citizens Advice advises that if your supplier goes bust, you should not switch tariff or supplier until your account has moved to the new supplier, because switching earlier can make it harder to get money you are owed. It also advises comparing as many suppliers as possible and asking for the full terms and conditions.
findings.limitations: No source read here covers supplier financial-resilience checks (for example Ofgem's financial responsibility or capital adequacy rules, credit ratings, or customer-service league tables). This finding is only about what the sources say on supplier choice and supplier failure.

findings.claim: Half-hourly settlement reform affects business electricity customers. Suppliers are migrating meters to market-wide half-hourly settlement (MHHS), so settlement will use actual half-hourly consumption rather than estimates or monthly readings.
findings.evidence: Elexon (page updated 2026-09-07): MHHS means settlement is based on "actual consumption for each half-hour of the electricity day, in place of estimates or monthly readings". Suppliers began migrating customers' meters from 22 October 2025. Elexon expects to have accepted about 80 per cent of meters by October 2026 and to complete implementation in May 2027. Key milestones: an 18-month migration for Unmetered Supplies and Advanced Metering Systems, which "are normally used by larger non-domestic consumers", starting 22 October 2025; an 18-month migration for smart and non-smart meters, also starting 22 October 2025; full transition complete 7 May 2027; and a cut-over to a shorter settlement timetable on 2 July 2027. Settlement currently takes 14 months and is planned to drop to four months. Elexon says granular data lets suppliers develop products that reward flexible use.
findings.limitations: This is an industry-facing Elexon page, not customer-facing guidance. It does not say how MHHS changes business contract prices or what customers must do, and it gives no customer-specific meter or contract-capacity guidance. The page does not cover contract capacity, usage-data preparation or purchase timing.

findings.claim: Green or renewable tariff claims can be checked against the REGO scheme. A REGO certificate shows that one MWh of electricity was generated from renewable sources, and suppliers must disclose their fuel mix annually.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: the REGO scheme "provides transparency to consumers about the proportion of electricity that suppliers source from renewable electricity". One REGO is issued per megawatt hour (MWh) of eligible renewable output. The primary use is Fuel Mix Disclosure (FMD), which requires licensed GB electricity suppliers to disclose to potential and existing customers the mix of fuels (coal, gas, nuclear, renewable, other) used to generate the electricity they supply. Ofgem administers the scheme for GB on behalf of the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. EU Guarantees of Origin are no longer recognised for GB FMD, FIT annual levelisation or CfD from the disclosure period beginning 1 April 2023.
findings.limitations: The Ofgem page explains the REGO scheme and FMD but does not give business-specific advice on verifying a supplier's green tariff, such as whether a tariff is REGO-backed. No ASA or CMA green claims guidance was read. The page shows no date.

findings.claim: ESOS (the Energy Savings Opportunity Scheme) is a compliance obligation for qualifying large undertakings that involves energy audits and a notification to the Environment Agency. It is separate from the choice of energy contract, though ESOS audits use measured consumption data.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK ESOS phase 3 guidance (Environment Agency as UK scheme administrator, last updated 2026-07-30): qualification is based on status on the qualification date. A qualifying organisation must carry out energy audits, or use alternative compliance routes (ISO 50001, DEC, GDA), complete an ESOS report, have a director review the findings, and submit a notification of compliance through the online system. Audits must be based, so far as reasonably practicable, on verifiable consumption data measured in energy units (not spend) over 12 consecutive months, and energy audits must be reviewed by an ESOS lead assessor unless total energy consumption is under 40,000 kWh. EPCs are not a valid compliance route. The page says the remaining phase 3 deadline is to submit the second progress update report by 5 December 2026, and refers readers to separate Phase 4 guidance for the current qualification and compliance requirements. Participating in other schemes does not automatically count as ESOS compliance.
findings.limitations: I read only the phase 3 guidance, which says phase 4 requirements (including the 2026 amendment to the regulations) are in separate guidance that I did not open. I therefore make no claim about the phase 4 qualification date, deadlines or thresholds. The page does not define a "large undertaking" in the extract shown.

findings.claim: Timing and data preparation before signing: know the contract end date and notice position, start renewal work early, and have accurate consumption information ready. This avoids defaulting to expensive out-of-contract or deemed rates and affects quotes and broker commission.
findings.evidence: GLCG advises identifying the contract end date and notice period and starting to look for a new deal at least three to six months in advance, using smart meter data to understand usage patterns. Citizens Advice says the supplier should contact microbusinesses about 3 months before the end of a fixed term, and that customers need to check contract terms, end date, standing charges, unit costs and annual usage when preparing to switch. Ofgem's TPI guidance says commission is based on consumption, so if actual use exceeds the estimate the customer pays on actual consumption, and estimates should be as accurate as possible. Ofgem also says suppliers can decide whether to supply based on size of supply or credit rating.
findings.limitations: The 3–6 month figure is a commercial broker recommendation (GLCG), not regulator guidance. No source read covers contract capacity (for example availability charges), or half-hourly meter-specific preparation.
